items.priority: Overview of the whole set (P2 HIGH to P5 MINIMUM)

items.body:
> **How to read this set:** Follow one patient through the operation. First understand what the surgeon and perfusionist need to do; then why bypass changes physiology; next how to protect the heart and brain, manage anticoagulation and safely return circulation to the patient; finally how to recognise and treat postoperative deterioration. Each chapter explains the mechanism first and then develops the anaesthetic decisions. Expanded procedural detail is integrated at the point where it matters. This remains a teaching text, not a summary of isolated learning outcomes.

## Why cardiac surgery is a distinct anaesthetic problem

- In most anaesthetics the circulation continues to deliver oxygen while surgery changes the patient’s physiology.
- In conventional on-pump cardiac surgery we deliberately stop, isolate or manipulate the heart, and transfer oxygen delivery to an extracorporeal circuit.
- The anaesthetist’s challenge is therefore not only to maintain haemodynamic stability: it is to hand the circulation safely to the bypass machine and later take it back.
- A patient with good haemodynamics before CPB may return with myocardial stunning, air, valve dysfunction, residual ischaemia, vasoplegia or coagulopathy.
- Successful separation is a diagnosis and a coordinated transition, not simply reducing pump flow.

The simplest mental model is **four phases:**

- 1. Before bypass: assess reserve, induce and monitor safely, prepare for bleeding, pacing and circulatory collapse.
- 2. On bypass: maintain cerebral/systemic oxygen delivery and anaesthesia while the perfusionist controls flow, oxygenation, gas exchange and temperature; the surgeon protects and repairs the heart.
- 3. Separating from bypass: warm, ventilate and fill the heart, restore rhythm and contractility, interrogate the repair, de-air, then progressively transfer flow back to the native circulation.
- 4. After bypass and in ICU: reverse anticoagulation, secure haemostasis, distinguish surgical bleeding from acquired coagulopathy and detect low cardiac output, tamponade, neurological injury and other early complications.

## A typical uncomplicated on-pump cardiac operation

| Stage | What happens | Why the anaesthetist cares |
|---|---|---|
| Induction and monitoring | Arterial line, appropriate venous access, GA, TOE/TEE where indicated, antibiotics | Coronary/valve disease makes hypotension, tachycardia and loss of rhythm dangerous. Establish baseline ventricular/valve findings. |
| Sternotomy and dissection | Median sternotomy, pericardial opening, conduit harvest when relevant | Bleeding, ischaemia, haemodynamic effects of manipulation; redo cases can injure heart before bypass is available. |
| Anticoagulation and cannulation | Systemic heparin, confirm adequate ACT, venous drainage and arterial return cannulae | Inadequate anticoagulation can clot the circuit. Aortic atheroma changes safe cannulation strategy. |
| Initiate CPB | Venous blood drains, pump sends it through oxygenator and heat exchanger to arterial system | Check systemic flow, arterial pressure, venous return, gas exchange and adequate depth of anaesthesia. |
| Clamp and cardioplegia | Aortic cross-clamp isolates coronary circulation, cardioplegia arrests/protects myocardium | Cardioplegia delivery and myocardial protection determine the ability to separate later. |
| Surgical repair | CABG distal/proximal anastomoses or valve replacement/repair | Need de-airing, venting and communication about lesions and residual pathology. |
| Reperfusion and separation | Cross-clamp removed, rewarming, ventilation/rhythm restored, flow returned to patient | This is when ventricular dysfunction, LVOT obstruction, RV failure and vasoplegia become visible. |
| Protamine and haemostasis | Heparin reversed, decannulation, drain placement, closure | Protamine reactions, residual heparin, fibrinolysis, platelet dysfunction and surgical bleeding. |
| Intensive care | Haemodynamic/ventilatory handover, warming, analgesia, extubation when safe | Early complication surveillance and goal-directed organ support. |

**Clinical thread:**

- Every later management choice should answer one question: **Is oxygen delivery limited by flow, arterial oxygen content, or the patient’s ability to use the flow?** During CPB, flow is largely machine-generated; after separation it depends on the heart.
- Severe anaemia, hypoxaemia, inadequate bypass flow, tamponade and low cardiac output can all reduce oxygen delivery by different mechanisms.

items.title: 2. Before bypass: assessment, risk, preparation and anxiolysis
items.los: SS_CS 1.3; SS_CS 1.7; SS_CS 1.15 (supporting knowledge for SS_CS 1.17 and SS_CS 1.19)
items.body:
## Preoperative assessment: find what may prevent safe induction or separation

- History and examination should establish symptoms, **functional reserve, coronary anatomy, ventricular and valve function, pulmonary vascular/right-ventricular status, cerebrovascular and renal disease**, frailty and bleeding risk.
- Review the operation and the reason for it: unstable angina needing CABG has different immediate risk from chronic severe AS requiring AVR.
- Ask about previous sternotomy, PCI, antiplatelets, anticoagulants, infection/endocarditis, pulmonary disease and previous problems with airway, bleeding or anaesthesia.

| Information | Why it changes the plan |
|---|---|
| Coronary angiography / CT | Left-main or proximal LAD disease, right-dominant circulation, graft targets, residual stenoses and potentially jeopardised territories. |
| TTE/TOE | LV/RV systolic function, diastolic filling, valve severity, pulmonary pressure, effusion, shunt and aortic disease. Note baseline lesions before starting CPB. |
| ECG / rhythm / device | Recent ischaemia, conduction disease, AF, paced rhythm and the need for pacing/defibrillation. |
| FBC, creatinine/electrolytes, LFT/coagulation, group and screen | Anaemia, renal vulnerability, electrolyte-mediated arrhythmia, transfusion preparation and anticoagulation issues. |
| Carotid/aortic imaging when indicated | Prior stroke, carotid disease or heavily diseased aorta changes cerebral protection/cannulation. Screening is selective, not automatic. |
| Risk models: EuroSCORE II / STS | Support informed risk discussion but cannot replace lesion-specific physiological judgement. |

**Red flags requiring optimisation or a different plan:**

- Decompensated HF, recent ACS, rapid arrhythmia, active infection, critical anaemia, severe pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction, or a severely calcified ascending aorta.
- When time allows, address preoperative anaemia and iron deficiency, nutrition, smoking, diabetes and renal risk.
- Balance cessation of P2Y12 inhibitors against ACS/stent and urgent-surgery risk using a cardiology–surgical decision; use contemporary cardiac-surgery medication guidance rather than transplanting non-cardiac surgery rules.

## Anxiety and premedication (SS_CS 1.3)

- Cardiac patients may be frightened of sternotomy, CPB, postoperative ventilation, mortality or ICU care.
- Anxiety increases sympathetic drive, myocardial oxygen demand and blood pressure.
- **First-line treatment is information and reassurance:** explain the sequence, monitoring, analgesia, expectation of drains and ventilation, and the postoperative destination; invite specific questions and address misconceptions.
- Quiet surroundings, a familiar support person when possible, language/cultural support and psychological strategies can outperform reflex sedation.

- When pharmacological anxiolysis is appropriate, individualise a small oral/IV benzodiazepine dose or a short-acting titrated alternative according to age, frailty, airway/OSA, respiratory reserve, hepatic impairment and haemodynamics.
- An illustrative monitored option is midazolam 0.5–1 mg IV titrated, rather than a fixed standard dose; consider avoiding in older/frail patients at risk of delirium.
- Dexmedetomidine can provide anxiolysis/sympatholysis but may produce bradycardia/hypotension and is not a universal premedication.
- In unstable coronary disease or critical AS, even modest sedation can reduce respiratory drive or systemic pressure.
- Continue necessary anti-anginal therapy and plan analgesia and reassurance as part of a coherent strategy.

## Before induction: practical preparation

- **Team briefing:** surgeon, perfusionist and anaesthetist agree on cannulation, CPB plan, cardioplegia, temperature, major anticipated difficulties, rescue bypass/MCS and transfusion.
- **Monitoring:** standard ANZCA monitoring, ECG ST analysis, invasive arterial pressure (consider before induction), large-bore IVs, central venous access when appropriate, temperature at more than one site during CPB, urine output, TOF, arterial/venous blood gases and haemoglobin.
  - TOE is valuable for baseline ventricular/valve assessment and later de-airing/repair.
  - Cerebral NIRS/processed EEG as appropriate.
- **Rescue readiness:** blood and rapid infuser, cardioversion/defibrillation, pacing, vasoactive infusions, difficult airway equipment, availability of bypass for high-risk induction.
- **Induction:** choose smooth and titrated drugs rather than a rigid recipe.
  - Propofol may markedly reduce SVR; etomidate causes relatively little immediate haemodynamic depression but has disadvantages; ketamine may increase demand and can depress catecholamine-depleted hearts.
  - Opioid-based balanced anaesthesia and early vasopressor are common.
  - Select goals from the underlying lesion (CAD: avoid tachycardia/ischaemia; AS: preserve coronary perfusion; MR: avoid excessive afterload; severe RV failure: avoid PVR rise).

## Re-do cardiac surgery: why the first incision can be the most dangerous (SS_CS 1.15)

After previous sternotomy, the RV, right atrium, ascending aorta or patent coronary grafts may adhere directly beneath the sternum. Sternal re-entry can cause catastrophic haemorrhage or acute loss of graft flow **before chest exposure or central cannulation**. A left internal mammary-to-LAD graft may cross the operative field; clamping/injury can infarct a large territory.

**Preoperative:**

- Obtain previous operation and graft maps, CT to show sternum–heart/aorta/graft distances, echo and coronary assessment when indicated; identify anticoagulants and redo-associated bleeding risk.
- Agree a re-entry strategy, alternative arterial/venous cannulation and whether peripheral vessels should be exposed or cannulated **before** sternotomy in a very high-risk case.
- Anticipate axillary/femoral access risks; peripheral cannulation itself may cause bleeding, dissection or limb ischaemia.

**Intraoperative:**

- Large-bore access and blood immediately available, invasive pressure and skilled TOE, surgeon/perfusionist present for induction and re-entry.
- Avoid disrupting a patent mammary graft; plan cardioplegia around it.
- If major injury occurs, communicate immediately, compress/control bleeding, replace volume with blood, rapidly establish CPB using pre-agreed access and treat myocardial ischaemia.
- **Postoperative:** expect more bleeding, transfusion, prolonged CPB, RV dysfunction and longer ICU stay.
- BJA Education’s 2024 repeat-sternotomy review is especially valuable for this LO.

items.title: 3. The surgical procedures: what is actually being done
items.body:
## Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)

- CABG creates a conduit beyond a stenotic epicardial coronary artery.
- Common grafts are **LIMA→LAD**, radial artery and saphenous vein.
- The LIMA generally has excellent long-term patency; radial grafts may be prone to spasm, whereas vein grafts have greater long-term atherosclerotic failure.
- The surgeon selects targets based on anatomy, run-off and viability; a patent graft is no guarantee of adequate perfusion if distal disease is severe.

**On-pump CABG steps:**

- Sternotomy/conduit harvest → systemic heparinisation → aortic and venous cannulation → CPB → cross-clamp/cardioplegia → distal graft anastomoses on arrested myocardium → proximal anastomoses to ascending aorta when required (or composite graft strategy) → de-airing/reperfusion → wean/protamine/haemostasis/closure.
- A side-biting clamp for proximal grafts can itself embolise aortic plaque; anaortic techniques can reduce manipulation in selected patients.

**Off-pump CABG (OPCAB):**

- Following heparinisation, a mechanical stabiliser immobilises a small epicardial area while the heart continues beating.
- The surgeon positions/displaces the heart to access target vessels; an intracoronary shunt may maintain distal flow during the anastomosis.
- A standby pump/perfusionist and clear conversion trigger are essential.
- **Anaesthetic physiology:** heart displacement reduces venous return, impairs RV filling and worsens MR or regional ischaemia; loss of output is often greatest when exposing posterior/lateral targets.
- Use careful preload, position adjustments, judicious vasopressor/inotrope and TOE; communicate before destabilising manipulation.
- Rescue severe ischaemia by releasing displacement, restoring perfusion and converting to CPB when necessary.
- Avoid inappropriate large fluid loading just to maintain BP.

**On versus off pump—exam judgement:**

- Avoiding CPB may lessen aortic manipulation and short-term inflammation in selected cases, but trial evidence is mixed and operator experience/complete revascularisation matter.
- CORONARY found similar five-year major outcomes; ROOBY showed worse five-year survival for off-pump in its largely male veteran population.
- These do not justify saying one technique is universally superior.

## Anaesthetic plan for CABG: why each choice matters

**Preop:**

- Define unstable ischaemia, LV/RV dysfunction, antiplatelet/bleeding risk, aortic atheroma and ability to tolerate induction.
- Continue appropriate chronic anti-anginal therapy; establish antithrombotic plan.
- **Intraop:** minimise tachycardia and hypotension, maintain coronary perfusion, use ECG and TOE for regional function; anticipate haemodynamic change at mammary harvest, heart displacement and reperfusion.
- Heparinise before cannulation; ensure anaesthesia on bypass.
- After grafting, new regional wall-motion abnormality suggests graft-related ischaemia or air until evaluated.
- **Postop:** surveillance for bleeding, myocardial injury, arrhythmia, low output, respiratory dysfunction and safe antiplatelet restart.

## Building an anaesthetic plan for a CABG patient: link the coronary anatomy to the operation

- **The operation only makes sense if you know which myocardium is at risk.** Before induction, look at the angiogram rather than relying on a diagnosis of ‘three-vessel disease’.
- Left-main disease, critical proximal LAD stenosis and severe lesions supplying collateral-dependent myocardium mean that even a brief reduction in diastolic pressure may precipitate widespread ischaemia.
- Document previous infarct territories, LV ejection fraction and regional function; a normal global EF can coexist with a clinically important threatened territory.
- Ask whether the patient has ongoing angina at rest, pulmonary oedema or escalating anti-anginal therapy, because these change the urgency and suitability of a leisurely elective preparation.

**Preoperative decisions:**

- Review aspirin and P2Y12 history (ACS, recent stent, planned urgency and bleeding risk), haemoglobin/iron status, renal function, diabetes including SGLT2 inhibitors, carotid/cerebrovascular symptoms and aortic atheroma.
- Aspirin is generally continued for isolated CABG unless there is a specific reason not to.
- When elective surgery allows a P2Y12 washout, the 2024 EACTS medication guideline suggests at least **3 days for ticagrelor, 5 for clopidogrel and 7 for prasugrel**.
- Those are cardiac-surgical bleeding-oriented intervals, not permission to interrupt recent-stent therapy without cardiology input.
- In ACS, an earlier operation may be safer than withholding revascularisation; a platelet-function assay may help estimate residual drug effect where available.
- Continue chronic beta-blockade and statin therapy when appropriate, but individualise RAAS-inhibitor/diuretic decisions to ventricular function and haemodynamics.
- The objective is not simply a normal BP; it is adequate coronary perfusion pressure during each phase of surgery. [EACTS perioperative medication guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae355).

**Why induction is hazardous:**

- Hypnosis removes sympathetic compensation and commonly reduces SVR; intubation creates a short catecholamine surge.
- Both directions can be harmful: a fall in aortic diastolic pressure reduces flow beyond a fixed stenosis, whereas tachycardia shortens diastole and raises oxygen consumption.
- Prepare arterial-pressure monitoring and vasopressors before induction, titrate opioid/hypnotic doses to the patient, and treat a new ST change together with BP and TOE findings.
- A single absolute heart-rate target is less useful than preserving the patient’s known tolerated rate while avoiding abrupt tachycardia and bradycardia with low output.

**Before cross-clamping:**

- Mammary-artery harvest, manipulation and sternotomy can change loading and provoke ischaemia.
- When the surgeon places an aortic cannula or cross-clamp, the team should already have agreed whether the ascending aorta is suitable for instrumentation; epiaortic ultrasound can be more sensitive than palpation for dangerous plaque.
- An arterial line in a radial artery used for graft harvest requires an agreed alternative (usually contralateral arterial access).
- Baseline TOE should record LV/RV function, valve pathology, regional wall motion and aortic findings, so changes after reperfusion can be recognised as new.

- **After grafting, interpret the TOE in the light of the anatomy.** A new anteroseptal RWMA after LIMA–LAD grafting suggests inadequate LAD perfusion, air, graft kinking/spasm or anastomotic failure; the relevant response is to restore perfusion and inspect the graft, not merely increase adrenaline.
- Inferior dysfunction may indicate RCA/PDA territory ischaemia or an RV problem.
- Reperfusion arrhythmias, graft spasm, bleeding and temperature/electrolyte disturbances can coexist.
- Effective de-airing and graded separation are essential.
- Postoperatively, distinguish expected post-cardiac-surgery troponin elevations from graft-related MI using clinical deterioration, ECG, serial values, echo and sometimes emergency angiography.

## Off-pump CABG: follow the haemodynamics as the heart is moved

Off-pump surgery is not simply ‘CABG without the pump’. The surgeon still needs a nearly motionless target, achieved with a stabiliser, while the rest of the heart beats in an abnormal position. The most important anaesthetic skill is anticipating **which position impairs which cardiac chamber**.

| Surgical moment | Typical physiological problem | First response and rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior LAD anastomosis | Local coronary occlusion and ischaemia, generally less displacement | Control HR/BP, watch ST and regional function; intracoronary shunt if needed. |
| Lateral wall / obtuse marginal target | Verticalisation/compression reduces RV inflow, twists the heart and may increase MR | Ask surgeon to reduce displacement immediately if output falls; inspect with TOE, restore perfusion pressure, use small fluid increments only if truly underfilled. |
| Inferior/posterior target | Marked heart elevation may obstruct venous return/RVOT and trigger arrhythmia | Optimise positioning and stabiliser, maintain preload and coronary perfusion, use vasoactive support as a bridge to completing the anastomosis. |
| Intracoronary snare/anastomosis | Brief regional ischaemia and electrical instability | Monitor ST/RWMA; release occlusion or use shunt if unsafe; maintain readiness for urgent CPB conversion. |

- An apparently low arterial pressure during displacement may reflect **mechanical impediment to filling or ejection**, so litres of crystalloid are inappropriate.
- The anaesthetist should tell the surgeon promptly if there is loss of waveform/pulsatility, severe ST change, VT/VF or sustained reduced output.
- Relieving displacement is often the fastest effective treatment.
- Other reasons to convert to CPB are ongoing ischaemia despite manoeuvres, refractory arrhythmia, inability to expose targets safely, or incomplete revascularisation.
- Trial findings (CORONARY and ROOBY) do not support declaring off-pump universally better; expertise, patient anatomy and completeness of grafting matter.

## Aortic valve replacement (AVR)

**Procedure:**

- Aortic cannulation and CPB → cross-clamp/antegrade or retrograde cardioplegia → transverse aortotomy → excise native valve/debride annulus → size and implant mechanical or bioprosthetic valve → close aortotomy/de-air → reperfuse and assess prosthetic function by TOE.
- A heavily calcified annulus risks embolisation and conduction-system injury; annular enlargement or aortic root work may be required.
- Some minimally invasive approaches use peripheral cannulation.

**Preop:**

- Severe AS has concentric LVH, high LVEDP and limited coronary reserve; preserve sinus rhythm and perfusion.
- Severe AR is volume-loaded, with risk of low DBP and coronary perfusion; avoid excessive bradycardia/afterload.
- **Intraop:** carefully titrate induction; obtain arterial monitoring before induction in severe disease; assess ventricular function and other valves on TOE.
- **Separation:** exclude prosthesis malposition/obstruction, paravalvular leak, new wall-motion abnormality and poor LV function; new AV block may require pacing.
- **Postop:** monitor conduction/heart block, bleeding, prosthetic valve function, low output and anticoagulation requirements.
- A mechanical prosthesis requires lifelong vitamin K antagonist treatment; a bioprosthesis has a different protocol and may still need anticoagulation for AF or another indication.

## Aortic valve replacement: how the operative steps relate to specific hazards

**Before surgery, distinguish AS from AR:**

- Severe AS produces a small, thick, stiff LV with high filling pressure and a narrow coronary perfusion reserve; induction hypotension and loss of atrial contraction can cause collapse.
- Chronic severe AR produces LV volume loading, often low diastolic aortic pressure and a large compliant ventricle; excessive bradycardia lengthens diastole and can increase regurgitation.
- An acutely insufficient aortic valve may instead cause fulminant pulmonary oedema without time for remodelling.
- These are different anaesthetic problems even though both require AVR.

**Surgical sequence and implications:**

- (1) sternotomy, heparin, aortic and venous cannulation
- (2) aortic cross-clamp and tailored cardioplegia (antegrade delivery may be ineffective in severe AR because cardioplegia runs back into the LV; retrograde coronary-sinus delivery or selective ostial cardioplegia may be needed)
- (3) aortotomy, excision of calcific valve tissue, annular debridement and sizing
- (4) placement/suturing of a mechanical or tissue prosthesis, occasionally with annular/root enlargement
- (5) aortotomy closure, de-airing, unclamping, reperfusion and TOE assessment.
- Each extra annular procedure lengthens ischaemic time.
- Calcium or tissue debris can embolise; injury near the membranous septum/AV node may cause complete heart block, so pacing must be ready.

**After implantation the loading conditions have changed:**

- Relieving AS suddenly lowers LV afterload, but the hypertrophied myocardium may still be stiff and ischaemia-prone.
- AR correction removes diastolic volume overload and may unmask underlying LV impairment.
- In a patient who cannot separate from bypass, examine prosthesis seating and leaflet excursion, transvalvular Doppler gradient under appropriate flow, paravalvular regurgitation, coronary ostial obstruction, ventricular function and intracardiac air.
- A high calculated gradient may represent prosthesis–patient mismatch, excessive flow or measurement error; a new severe leak or restricted leaflet is a surgical question.
- After surgery, watch for AV block, atrial/ventricular arrhythmia, bleeding, early prosthetic dysfunction and anticoagulation requirements.

**Choosing the prosthesis is part of the anaesthetic story:**

- Mechanical valves generally last longer but require lifelong VKA anticoagulation with valve-specific INR targets; bioprostheses avoid lifelong VKA for the prosthesis alone but can degenerate and may still require anticoagulation for AF or another indication.
- Tissue choice is not determined by a single age cutoff; it reflects lifetime intervention, patient preference, pregnancy plans, bleeding risk and ability to maintain therapeutic INR. [2025 ESC/EACTS valve guideline](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488).

## Mitral valve replacement (MVR)

**Procedure:**

- Establish CPB with suitable atrial access (often left atriotomy via interatrial groove, or transseptal approach) → inspect leaflets/subvalvular apparatus → repair if feasible or excise diseased tissue while preserving chordae when possible → implant valve → close atrium/de-air → TOE assessment.
- Preserving the subvalvular apparatus helps maintain LV geometry and function.
- In mitral **repair**, annuloplasty ring and leaflet/chordal techniques preserve the native valve; TOE examines residual MR and systolic anterior motion (SAM).

**Preop:**

- Significant MS causes pulmonary hypertension, AF and RV strain; avoid tachycardia, hypoxaemia and hypercapnia.
- MR creates a low-impedance LA outlet: an apparently normal EF can hide LV dysfunction.
- **Intraop:** plan RV protection and haemodynamics before and after correction.
- **After repair/replacement:** elimination of a regurgitant outlet increases effective LV afterload and can reveal acute LV dysfunction; SAM/LVOTO is particularly relevant after repair and is worsened by inotropes, hypovolaemia and low SVR.
- Diagnose with TOE rather than reflex escalation of catecholamines.
- **Postop:** monitor low output, atrial arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, prosthetic function and anticoagulation.

- **Exam comparison:** CABG’s immediate threat is ischaemia/graft failure; AVR adds afterload/diastolic and conduction problems; mitral surgery adds pulmonary vascular/RV stress, afterload mismatch and repair-related LVOTO. The same hypotensive BP can represent completely different pathophysiology in each.

## Mitral valve surgery: why repair and replacement must be distinguished

- The atrial and ventricular sides of the mitral valve are connected by annulus, papillary muscles and chordae.
- **Preserving this apparatus helps preserve LV geometry**; therefore, an anatomically durable repair is often preferred over replacement for suitable degenerative MR.
- Repair may include annular ring placement, neochordae, leaflet resection/sliding plasty or commissural work.
- Replacement requires excising native tissue and securing the prosthesis while preserving chordal attachments where feasible.

**Surgical sequence:**

- After CPB and cross-clamping, enter the left atrium through the interatrial groove or transseptally, inspect the valve, perform planned repair/replacement, close the atrium while removing intracardiac air, release the cross-clamp and assess the result under normalised preload/afterload.
- The surgeon may re-cross-clamp if significant residual regurgitation, stenosis, systolic anterior motion (SAM), injury or prosthetic malfunction remains.
- TOE can demonstrate mechanism, leaflet coaptation, residual MR, transmitral gradient, ventricular function, pulmonary venous flow and aortic-valve continuity.

**Mitral stenosis before surgery:**

- Impaired LA emptying raises LA, pulmonary venous and sometimes pulmonary arterial pressures; the RV may be chronically pressure-loaded.
- Tachycardia increases the diastolic transmitral gradient, and AF can produce both low flow and rapid pulmonary congestion.
- Prefer a controlled rate, sinus rhythm when possible, adequate but not excessive filling, and avoidance of hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis that raise PVR.
- Mechanical pressure gradients are flow- and rate-dependent; don’t interpret an isolated number without the valve area, rhythm and clinical context.

**Mitral regurgitation before surgery:**

- The LV ejects into both aorta and low-resistance LA.
- The measured LVEF may appear preserved because some ejection is backwards; **an EF around 60% may already represent impaired LV function in severe chronic primary MR**.
- Avoid excessive afterload and bradycardia while preserving forward output.
- Pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction and AF are important risk modifiers.

**Immediately after correction:**

- The LV can no longer offload into the LA, so effective impedance to ejection increases.
- A stunned or previously decompensated LV may now fail (afterload mismatch) despite a technically satisfactory repair.
- Distinguish this on TOE from residual MR or coronary injury.
- Following repair, a small hyperdynamic LV with anterior leaflet motion towards the septum, an LVOT gradient and posteriorly directed MR points to **SAM-associated LVOTO**.
- The solution is to reduce provoking contractility/tachycardia, restore afterload, correct genuine underfilling and consider surgical revision—not reflex high-dose inotropes.
- When replacing a calcified/rheumatic valve, anticipate atrioventricular groove injury, circumflex coronary compromise and residual obstruction.
- At the end, document residual regurgitation, gradients, ventricular function and rhythm as the ICU baseline.

## The first postoperative day differs by operation

- A CABG patient needs prompt assessment of recurrent regional ischaemia, graft-related failure, bleeding, postoperative AF and appropriate antiplatelet therapy.
- An AVR patient has particular vulnerability to new conduction block and prosthetic obstruction/leak.
- A mitral patient may require careful LV/RV support and assessment for pulmonary hypertension, afterload mismatch or SAM.
- **Shared risks** remain tamponade, low cardiac output, coagulopathy, ventilation-related RV effects, AKI and neurological complications.
- Immediate ICU handover should therefore include the actual procedure and the post-bypass TOE findings, not simply ‘uncomplicated cardiac surgery’.

items.title: 4. Cardiopulmonary bypass: make the machine understandable
items.body:
## What a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit does

- CPB is a **temporary extracorporeal cardiopulmonary circulation**.
- Systemic venous blood passes via right atrial/two-stage or bicaval cannulae to a venous reservoir.
- A roller or centrifugal pump propels blood through a membrane oxygenator and heat exchanger and returns it via an arterial filter/cannula (usually ascending aorta).
- Suction, vent and cardioplegia systems are supplementary circuits; their contents, gas exchange and air risk require special attention.

![CPB circuit diagram](set13-fig1.png)

Figure 1. The CPB circuit: blood flows from venous drainage through reservoir, pump and oxygenator to arterial return.

**Flow diagram:**

- Patient veins → venous cannula/reservoir → pump → membrane oxygenator + heat exchanger → arterial filter → aortic cannula → patient systemic arteries.
- The surgeon can therefore empty/arrest the heart while organs are perfused.
- In a conventional open-reservoir CPB circuit, blood–air/synthetic surface exposure, haemodilution and activated coagulation/inflammation are important; modern mini-circuits reduce some exposures but create different volume/air-handling constraints.

| Component | Function | Failure / exam implication |
|---|---|---|
| Venous drainage/reservoir | Receives venous return; buffers volume and allows air separation | Poor drainage from cannula obstruction, air lock, malposition, hypovolaemia or inadequate height/vacuum; low reservoir = air risk. |
| Pump | Generates systemic flow independently of native ventricles | Roller pumps are positive-displacement; centrifugal output depends on preload/afterload and may permit reverse flow if mismanaged. |
| Membrane oxygenator + sweep gas | Adds O₂ and removes CO₂ | **Blood flow** predominantly determines systemic O₂ delivery; **sweep-gas rate** mainly controls CO₂ removal; oxygenator FiO₂/area influence O₂ transfer. |
| Heat exchanger | Cools/warms blood | Avoid large gradients, hyperthermia and gaseous microemboli; multiple temperatures required. |
| Arterial filter/air detector | Reduces particles and bubbles | Air embolisation remains catastrophic if reservoir empties or line is compromised. |
| Cardioplegia / LV and aortic root vents | Arrests myocardium and prevents distension/air | Incorrect delivery, obstruction or inadequate venting causes ischaemia/LV distension and later failure to wean. |

## Bypass flow, oxygen delivery and why haematocrit matters

- A typical adult full-flow starting prescription is **2.2–2.4 L/min/m²** indexed to body surface area, adjusted to temperature, haemoglobin, venous saturation, lactate, oxygen delivery and cerebral monitoring rather than treated as an immutable target.
- **DO₂ = pump flow × arterial O₂ content;** in common units DO₂ (mL/min) ≈ Q (L/min) × CaO₂ (mL/dL) × 10. Arterial oxygen content depends mainly on haemoglobin and saturation; dissolved oxygen contributes relatively little.
- Thus a normal arterial PaO₂ does **not** exclude inadequate oxygen delivery after haemodilution or low pump flow.

- For a practical example: at Hb 80 g/L (8 g/dL) and SaO₂ 100%, CaO₂ is only about 10.7 mL/dL.
- A flow of 4.5 L/min delivers roughly 480 mL O₂/min; lower Hb or inadequate flow rapidly reduces reserve.
- Goal-directed perfusion protocols commonly seek an indexed DO₂ above approximately **280 mL/min/m²** as an association-based risk threshold for AKI; it is not a universal safe guarantee or a license to transfuse solely to reach a number.
- Integrate mixed venous saturation, lactate, haemodynamics, metabolic temperature and local protocol.

- **MAP on bypass** is affected by pump flow and systemic vascular resistance.
- Many centres aim roughly **50–80 mmHg**, individualised for cerebrovascular disease, autoregulation, metabolic need and high-risk organs; evidence does not justify one universal high MAP target.
- Lack of pulsatility does not necessarily mean absent perfusion.
- A low MAP with adequate flow, oxygen delivery and reassuring monitoring may represent low SVR, whereas low flow with a reassuring MAP can still be dangerous.

## Set the pump flow from oxygen delivery, not from a reassuring MAP alone

- Once the venous lines are draining and the arterial line is returning blood, it is easy to become falsely reassured by a normal arterial pressure.
- **The pump controls flow, but vasoconstriction controls much of the measured pressure.** A patient can have MAP 70 mmHg and inadequate organ oxygen delivery if the bypass flow, haemoglobin or oxygenator performance is poor.
- Conversely, a low MAP with apparently adequate flow may represent vasoplegia; simply increasing the pump flow will not always solve it.

The relationship to explain in a viva is:

- **Systemic oxygen delivery (DO₂) = pump blood flow × arterial oxygen content**, where arterial oxygen content is dominated by Hb-bound oxygen (approximately 1.34 × Hb [g/dL] × SaO₂, plus a small dissolved component).
- On CPB, index DO₂ to body surface area because patients of different size need different flow.
- For example, with Hb 8 g/dL, SaO₂ 100% and pump flow 2.4 L/min/m², indexed DO₂ is roughly 260 mL/min/m² before the dissolved component.
- Increasing flow or avoiding haemodilution improves DO₂; raising MAP with a vasopressor without improving delivery may not.

- **Typical adult flow** is often started around **2.2–2.6 L/min/m²** at normothermia, adjusted for temperature, metabolic requirements, Hb, venous saturation, lactate and clinical conditions.
- The current European CPB guideline recommends goal-directed perfusion that limits time at low DO₂ and suggests a lower indexed DO₂ threshold of approximately **280–300 mL/min/m² during normothermic CPB**, to reduce early AKI risk.
- This is a practical target, not an absolute individual survival cutoff, and measurement methods vary.
- Avoid treating the usual ‘flow index’ as a substitute for patient-specific oxygen delivery. [2024 CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947607/).

**Physiological variables to follow together:**

- Circuit flow and arterial line pressure, calculated indexed DO₂, haemoglobin/haematocrit, arterial/venous gases and SvO₂, temperature, lactate trend, urine output and regional cerebral oximetry where used.
- A falling venous saturation can mean increasing extraction from inadequate DO₂, high metabolic demand (e.g. rewarming), a sample/monitor fault or shunting; interpret it alongside those variables rather than transfusing automatically.

## PaCO₂, pH and temperature: what the perfusionist is controlling

- The oxygenator gas blender determines oxygen transfer and the gas sweep largely determines CO₂ clearance; the pump sets systemic blood flow.
- Increasing gas FiO₂ cannot compensate for zero/low systemic pump flow, and increasing sweep does not increase arterial Hb concentration.
- The physiological role of carbon dioxide is especially important because PaCO₂ alters cerebral arteriolar tone and cerebral blood flow.

- **Alpha-stat** analyses arterial blood gases as measured at 37°C without temperature correcting the target.
  - At hypothermia, in-vivo PaCO₂ is lower and pH higher than the displayed 37°C value; this tends to preserve autoregulation and protein charge state.
  - Adult CPB commonly employs alpha-stat, especially when atheroembolism risk is important.
- **pH-stat** adds CO₂ during cooling so that the temperature-corrected pH is about 7.40 and PaCO₂ about 40 mmHg. Cerebral vasodilation increases flow, cooling uniformity and potentially the distribution of gaseous/particulate emboli.
  - It is used selectively in paediatric and some deep-cooling contexts, not as a universal adult default.

Use these terms accurately: the technique concerns **how blood gases are interpreted and managed during temperature change**, not which ventilator setting is used before bypass. Discuss arterial blood gas sampling in terms of the centre’s protocol, since real-time blood gas systems and lab measurements differ.

## Haemodilution, inflammation and the body’s response

- The circuit is primed with crystalloid/colloid, diluting RBC, plasma clotting factors and platelets.
- The exposure of blood to artificial surfaces, suctioned mediastinal blood, surgical trauma and reperfusion activates contact, complement, cytokine and coagulation pathways.
- Consequences include **vasoplegia, capillary leak, platelet dysfunction, fibrinolysis, haemolysis and organ injury**.
- Systemic hypothermia reduces metabolic demand but also slows enzyme/drug clearance, alters coagulation and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve.
- Rewarming increases metabolic demand again; apparent stability while cold can conceal inadequate oxygen delivery.

- The kidney is vulnerable to reduced DO₂, haemolysis/pigment injury, inflammation, venous congestion and pre-existing CKD.
- Brain injury arises from embolism (air/atheroma), hypoperfusion and inflammatory/metabolic factors rather than a single mechanism.
- Good perfusion is therefore a balance of **adequate oxygen delivery, avoidance of emboli, temperature control and avoiding unnecessary blood–surface exposure**.

## Initiating CPB safely: a closed-loop communication sequence

- **1.** Confirm circuit checks, oxygen source/sweep, priming, arterial line/pressure monitoring, air management, blood availability, cannulation plan and emergency backup.
- **2.** Administer systemic heparin and **verify adequate anticoagulation** before any CPB flow (the details and ACT limitations are in Chapter 5).
- **3.** Under direct surgeon–perfusionist–anaesthetist communication, confirm arterial/venous cannula placement and perfusion pressure; start venous drainage and pump flow gradually, watching reservoir level, MAP, air detectors and venous pressures.
- **4.** Transition ventilation and anaesthesia to on-bypass practice: lung ventilation may be reduced/stopped by agreement, while oxygen delivery and CO₂ clearance are managed by the oxygenator. Ensure an explicit **IV/volatile anaesthetic delivery route** to prevent awareness as pulmonary uptake changes.
- **5.** Maintain indexed flow, temperature and gas exchange; monitor ACT, ABG, haematocrit, lactate, NIRS and urine output; regularly communicate haemodynamic and cerebral concerns.

- **A classic critical incident:** high arterial-line pressure but low effective patient flow may mean cannula kink/malposition or aortic dissection; simply increasing pump speed can worsen injury. Low reservoir/air alarm requires immediate communication and perfusionist-led clamping/stopping according to the emergency checklist, not reflex increased suction.

## Anaesthesia during CPB (SS_CS 1.17)

- The patient’s lungs may no longer exchange much gas with systemic circulation; **volatile agents delivered only into the ventilator may not maintain anaesthesia**.
- Volatile agents can instead be delivered through an appropriately designed, scavenged oxygenator vapour system, or an IV infusion can be used.
- Drug concentrations and clinical response change with haemodilution, protein binding, sequestration into circuit, altered cerebral blood flow and hypothermia; rewarming changes clearance.
- Neuromuscular blockade prevents movement but does not prevent awareness.
- Use a clear infusion/vaporiser plan, consistent pump checks and processed EEG where appropriate, recognising EEG changes with hypothermia and circulatory arrest.
- BIS may read very low when cold even without a proportionate change in hypnotic drug delivery.

**Ventilation:**

- While full CPB is established, local strategies range from apnoea with low-level CPAP to low tidal-volume ventilation; clinical outcome evidence does not support one universal method.
- Before separation, recruit gently, re-establish oxygenation and ventilation, and avoid excessive airway pressure that would compromise RV output.
- Always agree switching the ventilator off/on with perfusion and surgery.

## Anaesthesia does not stop when circulation is outsourced

- Hypnotic delivery can be interrupted by failure to connect the volatile supply to the oxygenator or by disconnected IV infusions when operating-room lines are reorganised.
- The patient is paralysed, and pump hypothermia may suppress EEG, so **absence of movement or a low BIS alone cannot confirm adequate anaesthesia**.
- Document where the volatile agent enters the oxygenator, verify scavenging (operating-room occupational safety), or use an independent IV hypnotic infusion with a reliable route.
- Altered volume of distribution, circuit adsorption and temperature affect pharmacokinetics.
- Reconfirm delivery during initiation, immediately after changes in perfusion configuration, and at rewarming/separation.

- These details are why pump induction is a three-person handover: surgeon confirms cannulation and readiness, perfusionist confirms safe venous return/flow/gas exchange, and anaesthetist confirms anticoagulation, anaesthesia, pressure monitoring and patient oxygen delivery.
- The same closed-loop communication is required before arterial cross-clamping and before reducing pump flow for separation.

## Complications during bypass: recognise the mechanism

- **Poor venous drainage:** malposition, kinking, hypovolaemia, air lock, obstructed SVC/IVC, inadequate cannula size; troubleshoot cannulas, heart filling, reservoir and vacuum rather than indiscriminate fluid.
- **High arterial pressure in circuit / low flow:** kink, obstruction, aortic cannula malposition or dissection; immediately evaluate patient and circuit.
- **Poor oxygenation/CO₂ removal:** check oxygenator gas supply/FiO₂/sweep, membrane function, blood flow and saturation sampling sites; oxygenator change may be necessary.
- **Air embolism:** stop/secure inflow as appropriate, prevent further delivery, identify source, de-air and support organ perfusion with team emergency protocol.
- **Circuit clotting:** inadequate anticoagulation or failure; maintain perfusion safety, obtain ACT/heparin measurements and change circuit components if required.
- **Unexpected cerebral NIRS fall:** exclude sensor/technical failure; assess pump flow, MAP, Hb, PaCO₂, SaO₂, cannula or arch-vessel malperfusion and temperature; address each cause rather than assuming isolated hypotension.

## Three dangerous technical emergencies on CPB

- 1. Inadequate venous drainage.
- The arterial pump may be delivering more blood than is returning to the reservoir, so the reservoir falls and systemic air entry becomes a catastrophe.
- First alert the perfusionist/surgeon, reduce output as needed to preserve circuit safety, assess cannula position and kinking, venous obstruction, excessive suction or vacuum-assisted drainage, patient positioning and true volume depletion.
- A low CVP is not diagnostic when the venous cannula actively drains the atrium.
- Repositioning the cannula or correcting the obstruction may restore drainage more effectively than giving fluid.

- 2. Arterial line obstruction or malperfusion.
- Rising post-oxygenator/arterial-line pressure together with falling systemic pressure suggests a kink, clamp, false-lumen cannulation or arterial cannula obstruction.
- Cannulating into an aortic dissection can deliver flow into the false lumen and compromise cerebral/visceral perfusion.
- Immediately stop unsafe escalation of pump pressure, communicate and check line/cannula, bilateral arterial pressure and NIRS changes.
- Imaging/TOE or direct surgical assessment and a new arterial cannulation plan may be required.

- 3. Massive air entry into the arterial circuit.
- Treat this as a team emergency, not a routine brief ‘air bubble’.
- Follow the perfusion emergency protocol to prevent further air delivery, secure the arterial line, stop/manage pump flow appropriately, identify and correct the source and use circuit air-handling/filtration procedures.
- The surgeon should assess aortic root and cerebral/coronary de-airing strategies.
- Prolonged unperfused time can be worse than the air event; rapid, coordinated restoration of safe flow is critical.
- Clinical neurological injury can appear only after rewarming/awakening.

items.title: 5. Anticoagulation, blood conservation and protamine
items.los: SS_CS 1.17 (anticoagulation, point-of-care testing, antifibrinolytics, protamine); SS_CS 1.18 (heparin resistance and HIT)
items.body:
## Why standard coagulation is inadequate for bypass

- The CPB circuit exposes blood to foreign surfaces and high shear; without anticoagulation, fibrin and platelet deposition may obstruct the oxygenator or arterial circuit and precipitate catastrophic embolism.
- **Unfractionated heparin (UFH)** is preferred because it acts rapidly, can be monitored at bedside and is antagonised by protamine.
- Heparin potentiates **antithrombin (AT)** inhibition of thrombin (IIa) and Xa, with effects on several other serine proteases.
- Its effect depends on adequate antithrombin, heparin-binding proteins and patient response.

- A common initial CPB heparin dose is **300–400 units/kg IV**, but the correct target is adequate anticoagulation on the chosen circuit/test, not a universally fixed number of units.
- Many conventional adult CPB services use **ACT >480 seconds** before cannulation and throughout; some use lower device-specific thresholds for heparin-coated circuits, different ACT technology or alternative protocols.
- Recheck after heparin, during prolonged CPB and when additional anticoagulant is given.
- A surprisingly high ACT may reflect hypothermia, haemodilution, thrombocytopenia or test artefact rather than sufficient true heparin activity.

## Plan haemostasis before the first heparin dose

Cardiac-surgical bleeding is difficult because **three problems overlap:** a surgeon may have an unligated vessel; CPB can consume/dilute/impair the haemostatic system; and the patient may already be receiving antithrombotic drugs. The correct approach is to anticipate all three rather than react to a large chest-drain output with indiscriminate plasma.

- **Preoperative patient blood management** means evaluating anaemia and its cause (iron deficiency, CKD, inflammation or B12/folate deficiency), defining aspirin/P2Y12/warfarin/DOAC exposure and last dose, estimating bleeding risk from redo surgery/complex aortic procedures, and establishing a crossmatch/cell-salvage plan.
- Treat iron deficiency when scheduling permits; avoid transfusing an asymptomatic anaemic patient simply to obtain a normal Hb without considering risks and timing.
- A formal MDT decision is required when urgent ACS-related CABG conflicts with platelet-inhibitor washout.
- The 2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient-blood-management guideline emphasises preoperative optimisation and patient-specific coagulation strategies. [Guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae352).

**During the operation, reduce avoidable loss:**

- Meticulous surgical haemostasis, minimally necessary bypass prime volume and haemodilution, cell salvage, suitable transfusion thresholds, normothermia, correction of hypocalcaemia and acidosis, and an antifibrinolytic strategy.
- Cell salvage does not reliably return platelets/coagulation factors; washed recovered RBCs improve oxygen-carrying capacity but do not replace targeted haemostatic therapy.
- The team must know whether autologous blood sequestered before CPB remains available for reinfusion after reversal.

## Monitoring: what the tests measure

| Test | What it tells you | Major limitations |
|---|---|---|
| ACT (activated clotting time) | Whole-blood clotting time after contact activator; rapid point-of-care assessment at high heparin levels | Altered by low platelets, low temperature, haemodilution, factors, device and activator; not a precise heparin concentration. |
| Heparin concentration / anti-Xa | More direct assessment of heparin exposure/effect where available | Methods and high-dose calibration differ; anti-Xa measures AT-dependent activity and may be less practical at full CPB levels. |
| aPTT | Helpful for conventional UFH outside CPB | Saturates at high heparin levels; generally unsuitable as sole monitoring on CPB. |
| TEG/ROTEM with heparinase comparison | Detects residual heparin and identifies fibrinogen/platelet/coagulation deficits during bleeding work-up | Not a substitute for adequately anticoagulating the circuit; VHA thresholds depend on cartridge and local algorithm. |
| FBC, fibrinogen, PT/INR, ionised Ca, ABG, temperature | Interpret the patient’s capacity to clot after CPB | Laboratory turnaround and assay artefacts; treat clinical bleeding, not numerical abnormalities alone. |

## Heparin resistance: do not just keep escalating blindly

**Definition:**

- Failure to reach the institution’s target ACT or measured heparin effect after a conventionally adequate dose.
- Mechanisms include AT deficiency/consumption (after previous heparin exposure, critical illness, sepsis or liver disease), high heparin-binding proteins, thrombocytosis/high fibrinogen, inflammation and test-related problems.
- Some patients have adequate heparin concentration despite a ‘short’ ACT.
- Always verify dose/administration, test function and whether the target is appropriate before labelling resistance.

**Stepwise approach:**

- (1) Recheck ACT and dosing; ensure heparin reached circulation.
- (2) Check heparin concentration or anti-Xa where available and distinguish true pharmacological resistance from ACT insensitivity.
- (3) Give additional UFH if indicated and reassess.
- (4) If AT deficiency is likely/persistent, administer **antithrombin concentrate**, or FFP if AT unavailable and clinically appropriate, with transfusion risks considered.
- (5) A patient with known HIT needs an **alternative anticoagulant**, not arbitrarily more heparin.
- Failure to establish safe anticoagulation is a reason not to initiate conventional CPB until a specialist plan is agreed.

## Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: two very different problems

- A postoperative platelet fall after CPB is common from dilution, consumption and inflammation; it does **not** by itself prove HIT.
- Immune HIT is caused by IgG directed at platelet factor 4–heparin complexes, activating platelets and generating **arterial and venous thrombosis** despite falling platelets.
- It classically appears **5–10 days** after heparin exposure, or sooner with recent sensitisation.
- A biphasic platelet pattern (initial CPB fall/recovery followed by a second fall) is more suspicious than the expected early CPB nadir.

**Diagnose systematically:**

- Apply the 4Ts pretest score (thrombocytopenia magnitude, timing, thrombosis, alternative explanations).
- If intermediate/high suspicion, stop all heparin sources—including flushes—and send PF4 immunoassay followed by a functional assay (e.g. serotonin-release assay) when available.
- Avoid testing every routine post-CPB platelet decline because false-positive antibody tests are common.
- Do **not** give prophylactic platelets routinely in active HIT without a special bleeding indication.

**Management:**

- Urgent haematology, non-heparin therapeutic anticoagulation when HIT is suspected and bleeding permits (often argatroban or bivalirudin; agent/dose adjusted for hepatic/renal function), ultrasound/investigation for thrombosis and a clear long-term anticoagulation plan.
- In urgent CPB during active HIT, **bivalirudin** is a leading alternative: direct thrombin inhibition independent of AT, short half-life (longer with renal dysfunction), no protamine reversal and risk of clot formation in stagnant blood because the drug is consumed locally.
- Perfusion must avoid stagnant reservoirs/lines and use a dedicated protocol.
- If elective cardiac surgery can be postponed until acute HIT resolves and antibodies fall, that is generally preferable; decisions in subacute/remote HIT are specialist and phase-specific.

## Heparin resistance and HIT: deeper decisions that distinguish good viva answers

- **Heparin resistance** can be a laboratory phenotype rather than true lack of anticoagulant effect.
- An ACT may be misleading if clotting-factor levels, temperature, platelet count or activator vary.
- A patient receiving 400 units/kg with an ACT below local target should not be connected to the pump until the team has determined why; verify correct IV administration, repeat with the correct sample and test cartridge, assess heparin concentration where possible and consider antithrombin deficiency.
- In documented antithrombin deficiency, **antithrombin concentrate is preferred** when available; FFP is an alternative but delivers a less concentrated product with more volume exposure.
- Simply doubling UFH repeatedly without diagnostic feedback risks bleeding and still may not resolve the issue.

- **HIT after cardiac surgery** is often misdiagnosed because the platelet count routinely falls soon after CPB.
- The immune syndrome usually presents **5–10 days** after heparin (rapid-onset if recently sensitised) and causes thrombosis despite low platelets.
- A **second fall after initial recovery** is especially suspicious.
- Use the 4Ts score to estimate pretest probability; low clinical probability argues strongly against indiscriminate anti-PF4 testing, because many patients form non-pathogenic antibodies after CPB.
- When probability is intermediate/high, stop all heparin products/flushes and urgently involve haematology for an alternative therapeutic anticoagulant and laboratory confirmation (immunoassay followed by a functional test where feasible).

**Why bivalirudin on bypass is special:**

- Unlike UFH it directly inhibits thrombin, does not require antithrombin and cannot be reversed by protamine.
- Blood that stagnates in a shunt or reservoir can clot because local drug concentration falls; the perfusionist must maintain flow and follow a dedicated circuit dosing/testing protocol.
- Argatroban (hepatic clearance) and bivalirudin (substantial proteolysis plus renal effects) have different implications with liver/renal dysfunction.
- Surgery for stable active HIT should be delayed if possible, whereas emergency surgery requires specialist risk acceptance and a detailed non-heparin bypass plan.
- The distinction between suspected HIT, confirmed HIT, subacute HIT and remote antibody-negative HIT changes what anticoagulant options are reasonable; not all phases justify the same blanket rule.

## Reversing heparin with protamine

- Protamine is a positively charged polypeptide that electrostatically binds negatively charged heparin, producing an inactive complex.
- It **does not reverse bivalirudin**.
- A conventional maximum neutralisation calculation is around **1 mg protamine for every 100 units of heparin**, but this may substantially overestimate requirements because heparin has been redistributed/metabolised.
- Current practice often uses measured heparin concentration and lower protamine:heparin ratios, such as ~0.6–1 mg per 100 units of relevant circulating heparin, rather than automatically neutralising every unit ever given.
- Give **slowly IV** with invasive BP monitoring and communication to surgeon/perfusionist.
- Excess protamine itself impairs platelet function and coagulation and can cause hypotension; more is not necessarily better.

**Protamine reactions: recognise three clinically important patterns.**

| Reaction | Mechanism and presentation | Immediate management |
|---|---|---|
| Rapid systemic hypotension | Vasodilation, especially with fast infusion | Stop/slow protamine, support MAP with vasopressor, assess bleeding/ventricular function; distinguish from anaphylaxis and haemorrhage. |
| Severe anaphylaxis/anaphylactoid reaction | Immune or non-IgE mediator release; hypotension, bronchospasm, rash/angio-oedema may occur | Stop protamine, call help, **adrenaline** per perioperative anaphylaxis algorithm, oxygen, appropriately titrated fluid, support circulation; consider re-heparinisation/return to CPB when required. |
| Acute pulmonary hypertension / RV failure | Complement/thromboxane-related pulmonary vasoconstriction, sudden high PAP, RV dilation, low LV filling and shock | Stop infusion, support systemic/RV coronary pressure, optimise oxygenation/ventilation/acidosis, consider pulmonary vasodilator and inotropy, re-establish CPB urgently if refractory. |

- **Risk factors** often cited include previous protamine exposure (including protamine-containing insulin), fish allergy and previous vasectomy, but these are imperfect predictors and not reliable reasons to presume a reaction.
- If suspected anaphylaxis, document chronology, take serial tryptase as clinically indicated and refer for specialist investigation.
- After reversal, assess the ACT/heparinase assay and bleeding rather than repeatedly dosing protamine solely for a mildly elevated ACT.
- Late ‘heparin rebound’ can reflect redistribution from tissues/circuit and should be interpreted with laboratory evidence and clinical bleeding.

## Protamine: think of three different physiology problems, not one allergy label

- If hypotension appears during reversal, pause the infusion and rapidly assess rhythm, TOE, arterial pressure, PAP/CVP if present, airway pressures, oxygenation and skin signs.
- **Simple rate-related vasodilation** produces systemic hypotension with relatively preserved ventricular contractility and no severe PVR surge.
- **Severe anaphylaxis** may produce vasoplegia and bronchospasm with or without rash under drapes.
- **Acute pulmonary vasoconstriction** produces a suddenly distended/failing RV, falling LV filling, rising PAP and profound systemic hypotension; this can become a circulation-threatening emergency even without cutaneous features.

- For vasodilation, stop/slow protamine and support the circulation
- For anaphylaxis, administer **adrenaline** and follow the ANZCA/ANZCOR perioperative algorithm
- For RV failure, oxygenate, correct hypoxia/acidosis/hypercarbia, provide perfusion-pressure support and discuss inhaled pulmonary vasodilator/reinstitution of CPB immediately.
- In a catastrophic reaction with bypass cannulas still present, return to CPB may save the patient while the reaction is treated.
- **Do not give an uncritical large crystalloid load to a dilated congested RV.** If inadequate reversal leaves unsafe bleeding, balancing a further protamine attempt against recurrence requires consultant-led discussion and alternative strategies.

## Why cardiac surgical patients bleed after bypass

- The patient can have **surgical bleeding** (anastomosis, cannulation, sternum) or **microvascular coagulopathic bleeding** (platelet dysfunction/consumption, reduced fibrinogen, dilutional factor deficiency, hyperfibrinolysis, hypocalcaemia, acidosis/hypothermia or excess heparin/protamine).
- These may coexist.
- Diffuse oozing from multiple raw surfaces suggests coagulopathy; brisk/continuous localised drain output, early haemodynamic instability or retained clot suggests a surgical source, even if coagulation tests are abnormal.

- **A logical blood-management pathway:**

- 1. Before surgery: correct anaemia/iron deficiency where time permits; review antiplatelets/anticoagulants, bleeding history and blood conservation consent. Group/crossmatch and assess transfusion need.
- 2. During surgery: meticulous haemostasis, minimise unnecessary haemodilution, cell salvage where appropriate, maintain temperature and ionised calcium, avoid excessive crystalloid and monitor haemoglobin/oxygen delivery.
- 3. Antifibrinolytic: **tranexamic acid (TXA)** inhibits plasminogen–fibrin interactions, reducing fibrinolysis.
  - Commonly used in cardiac surgery, but regimen varies and high exposures/renal impairment increase seizure risk.
  - **ATACAS** showed reduced transfusions/re-exploration but more postoperative seizures; choose renal-adjusted local dosing, avoid indiscriminate high-dose escalation.
- 4. After protamine: examine surgical field and chest drainage; send FBC/fibrinogen/INR and use **ROTEM/TEG-based algorithms** to direct treatment of actual bleeding.
  - Correct fibrinogen deficiency with cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate, platelet dysfunction/deficiency with platelets, coagulation-factor deficiency with plasma or selected concentrates per protocol.
  - Distinguish residual heparin using heparinase paired tests before giving more protamine.
- 5. Re-explore early: for suspected surgical source/tamponade rather than giving repeated haemostatic products and allowing ongoing haemorrhage.

**ROTEM interpretation example:**

- Prolonged clotting time (EXTEM CT) suggests coagulation factor deficiency or anticoagulant effect
- Reduced FIBTEM amplitude suggests inadequate fibrinogen contribution
- Low EXTEM amplitude relative to preserved FIBTEM suggests platelet contribution
- A correction of abnormalities in heparinase-modified channels suggests heparin effect.
- Numeric cutoffs and products are **instrument-, test- and institutional-algorithm-specific**.
- The 2025 ANZCA Blue Book chapter by Hegde and colleagues makes exactly this point: treat a **bleeding patient with a demonstrated deficit**, not every abnormal tracing.

## Tranexamic acid: why it works, and why dose still matters

- CPB activates endothelial and contact pathways and can increase conversion of plasminogen to plasmin.
- **Plasmin degrades cross-linked fibrin**, causing premature dissolution of newly formed clot.
- Tranexamic acid (TXA), a synthetic lysine analogue, blocks plasminogen/plasmin lysine-binding sites and inhibits fibrin binding and fibrinolysis.
- It therefore prevents clot breakdown; it does **not** reverse UFH or replace fibrinogen/platelets when these are deficient.

- The large **ATACAS** trial found less major bleeding/reoperation with TXA in coronary surgery, but more seizures; it did not demonstrate an overall mortality benefit.
- Convulsions are plausibly related to concentration-dependent CNS glycine and GABA-A receptor inhibition; high dose and renal impairment increase concern.
- **Do not memorise a single universal cardiac TXA regimen.** Centres use lower- or higher-dose schedules, sometimes an IV loading dose followed by infusion and/or pump-prime supplementation.
- Select dose and timing according to local cardiac protocol, renal function, seizure risk and the operation, rather than automatically adopting a dose from orthopaedic or obstetric surgery.
- Routinely distinguish prophylactic antifibrinolysis from therapeutic response to active hyperfibrinolytic bleeding. [ATACAS](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1606425).

## Treat post-bypass bleeding by locating the defective step in clot formation

- A patient bleeds briskly after protamine.
- The correct first question is **‘Is this a surgical source or diffuse coagulopathy?’** A persistently filling surgical field/one rapidly draining mediastinal tube can indicate a bleeding anastomosis; widespread oozing from cannulation sites suggests acquired haemostatic impairment.
- Either can coexist, so request early surgical inspection while sending appropriate blood tests.
- Examine actual blood loss, perfusion status, temperature, pH, ionised calcium and pre-existing antithrombotic exposure.

| Finding / investigation | What it suggests | Rational treatment (if clinically bleeding) |
|---|---|---|
| Heparinase and non-heparinase clotting traces differ substantially; ACT remains prolonged after protamine | Residual UFH or heparin rebound (consider also protamine excess and test interference) | Confirm with paired measurements/heparin assay, give **carefully titrated** additional protamine only when indicated; excessive protamine worsens bleeding. |
| Low FIBTEM functional fibrinogen or low Clauss fibrinogen | Fibrinogen depletion or impaired fibrin polymerisation | Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate per protocol; repeat the assay and check clinical response. |
| Poor TEG MA / ROTEM EXTEM clot firmness with adequate fibrin contribution | Reduced platelet number or function, including antiplatelet effect | Platelets if significant bleeding and a documented functional/quantitative deficit; consider P2Y12 exposure, hypothermia and high shear. |
| Prolonged clot initiation after excluding residual heparin | Coagulation-factor depletion | Plasma or selected factor concentrate according to validated protocol; beware prothrombotic rescue therapy. |
| Rapid late lysis on TEG/ROTEM | Hyperfibrinolysis | Confirm TXA exposure and dose, correct cause, give antifibrinolytic according to protocol. |
| Firm/near-normal viscoelastic clot but substantial chest-drain bleeding | Surgical source, platelet defect not measured by routine assay, local site bleeding | Return attention to surgeon and operative field; do not treat the monitor instead of the patient. |

**Interpretation caveat:**

- ROTEM EXTEM, INTEM, HEPTEM and FIBTEM are different assay channels.
- An institutional algorithm may use A5/A10 or MCF with validated thresholds; values are not interchangeable between instruments or centres.
- Viscoelastic tests can guide targeted treatment but cannot reliably diagnose every P2Y12-associated platelet defect.
- This is the practical point of the ANZCA Blue Book 2025 chapter by Hegde and colleagues on viscoelastic haemostatic assays: identify the deficient clot component and **choose the corresponding therapy**, rather than blindly giving one unit of every blood product. [ANZCA 2025 Blue Book](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-%28the-blue-book%29).

## Transfusion thresholds and the evidence

- For stable adult cardiac surgical patients, restrictive RBC strategies around Hb **75 g/L** have been supported by **TRICS III** (non-inferiority for major clinical outcomes versus liberal thresholds in the trial population).
- That is not a mandatory trigger in active shock, ongoing major haemorrhage or myocardial ischaemia.
- Balance Hb against active bleeding, oxygen delivery, SvO₂/lactate and clinical context.
- A normal ACT does not mean normal platelet function; a ‘normal’ fibrinogen before prolonged CPB does not guarantee adequacy after dilution.
- Avoid the common exam mistake of prescribing a fixed FFP–platelet–cryo package without assessing the bleeding phenotype and coagulation data.

- **Evidence anchors:** [Cartwright & Mundell, BJAEd 2023 Part 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003), [Part 2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.008), [2024 cardiac PBM guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12257489/), [2025 ANZCA Blue Book goal-directed haemostasis](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387).

## Transfusion decisions: an evidence-informed floor, not a reason to ignore physiology

- **TRICS III** supports restrictive RBC transfusion in many adults undergoing cardiac surgery: **Hb trigger 75 g/L** was non-inferior for a composite clinical outcome compared with a more liberal strategy, but this does not mean every patient with ongoing graft ischaemia, severe shock or poor DO₂ on pump must tolerate Hb 75. Assess bleeding rate, oxygen extraction, cerebral/somatic perfusion, coronary ischaemia and the ability to increase pump flow.
- More plasma or platelets are not substitutes for RBCs when the principal problem is oxygen-carrying capacity.
- Conversely, if the patient is euvolaemic with a reasonable Hb but is bleeding because of fibrinogen depletion, RBCs will not fix that mechanism. [TRICS III](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818).

**The endpoint of the bleeding algorithm is not normal blood tests: it is haemostasis and organ perfusion without avoidable transfusion harm.** After haemostatic therapy, repeat clinical assessment and selected tests. Reassess whether ongoing chest drainage warrants prompt surgical re-exploration rather than repeated product administration in ICU.

items.title: 6. Myocardial, cerebral and whole-body protection on bypass
items.body:
## Myocardial protection: how can an arrested heart survive?

- The heart needs ongoing ATP to maintain ion gradients, calcium handling and myocyte viability.
- Coronary flow is interrupted during aortic cross-clamping, so unprotected warm ischaemia rapidly causes ATP depletion, acidosis, intracellular Ca²⁺ accumulation, contracture and reperfusion damage.
- **Cardioplegia** chemically arrests the myocardium, usually in diastole using high extracellular potassium, while cooling and delivery of oxygenated substrate reduce metabolic demand. ‘Stopping the heart’ is not itself protection; it is the combination of rapid arrest, adequate distribution, appropriate temperature and intermittent replenishment that prevents damage.

| Strategy | Physiological effect | Clinical limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Antegrade cardioplegia via aortic root/coronary ostia | Physiological coronary direction; rapid uniform delivery with patent proximal arteries | Severe proximal stenoses or severe AR can impair distribution; aortic root delivery may leak into LV in AR. |
| Retrograde via coronary sinus | Perfuses many myocardial regions despite proximal stenosis; useful adjunct in severe coronary disease | RV/anterior territories may be less reliably protected; risk of coronary-sinus injury/overpressure. |
| Cold blood or crystalloid solutions | Cooling reduces O₂ demand, potassium arrest | Very cold techniques can affect microcirculation; re-dose as required. |
| Warm blood cardioplegia | Delivers O₂/substrate and supports metabolic recovery | Myocardium consumes more O₂ at higher temperature; requires reliable continuous/intermittent delivery. |
| Venting and topical cooling | Prevent LV distension and improve myocardial protection | LV distension raises wall stress and subendocardial demand even during bypass. |

- **After removing the clamp**, coronary reperfusion may cause ventricular fibrillation, transient stunning, hyperkalaemia from cardioplegia washout, oxidative stress or calcium-mediated injury.
- **Ischaemic preconditioning** describes brief, nonlethal ischaemia inducing endogenous protective pathways (mitochondrial signalling, kinase activation and altered reperfusion response), while postconditioning refers to brief interruptions around reperfusion.
- Although biologically attractive, clinical outcome benefits of anaesthetic/remote conditioning strategies have been inconsistent; do not claim a specific volatile agent guarantees cardiac protection.

## Myocardial protection in practice: match the delivery route to the operation

- After the aorta is cross-clamped the myocardium can no longer rely on normal coronary perfusion.
- **Cardioplegia converts an actively contracting, energy-consuming heart into a deliberately arrested heart** while providing some combination of cooling, substrate, oxygen and buffer.
- Potassium-rich solution depolarises cardiomyocytes and prevents normal action potential propagation; reduced cross-bridge cycling drastically reduces ATP demand, but basal membrane-pump and metabolic demand persist.
- Arrested myocardium is therefore protected, not metabolically inert.

- Antegrade cardioplegia travels through the aortic root into coronary ostia and is often efficient when the aortic valve is competent and coronary distribution permits it.
- Severe proximal coronary stenoses may impair delivery to threatened territories, and **severe aortic regurgitation** can divert root cardioplegia into the LV, distending it rather than perfusing the coronaries.
- Selective coronary ostial delivery or **retrograde coronary-sinus cardioplegia** then becomes valuable.
- Retrograde delivery is especially useful for areas beyond stenoses or during valve surgery, but perfuses the RV variably and depends on correct sinus cannulation; it does not replace careful visual assessment of myocardial protection.
- For a long clamp interval the team must know the redosing schedule, temperature and whether the perfusate is crystalloid or blood-based.

**Venting is itself myocardial protection:**

- When the heart is arrested, bronchial/coronary venous return and any aortic regurgitant flow may fill the LV.
- LV distension increases wall tension, subendocardial pressure and oxygen demand, worsens myocardial oedema and increases risk of impaired separation.
- A left-heart vent through the pulmonary vein/LA or aortic root (at the appropriate stage) prevents distension and facilitates de-airing.
- A suddenly full LV on TOE despite CPB is a signal to evaluate venting and valve incompetence, not automatically a reason to give diuretic or increase inotrope.

- **Reperfusion injury** adds to ischaemic injury when the clamp is removed.
- Oxygen-derived reactive species, sudden calcium influx, mitochondrial permeability-transition pore opening, endothelial dysfunction and inflammatory activation can cause myocardial stunning, rhythm disturbance and microvascular dysfunction even with technically successful grafts.
- Rewarm and reperfuse deliberately; check potassium and acid–base balance, treat ventricular fibrillation, support coronary perfusion pressure and distinguish transient stunning from persistent mechanical/graft obstruction.
- Ischaemic preconditioning and volatile ‘conditioning’ have attractive mechanisms but inconsistent hard-outcome clinical evidence, so they supplement—not replace—adequate cardioplegia, time management and perfusion.

## Aortic atheroma and safe cannulation

- A diseased ascending aorta is a major source of embolic stroke, especially during cannulation, cross-clamping, side-biting clamps and de-airing.
- Review aortic imaging and palpation/epiaortic ultrasound; **epiaortic ultrasound is particularly useful for identifying plaque not reliably appreciated by palpation or TOE** (distal ascending aorta has a TOE blind spot).
- Options include choosing a clean aortic site, axillary/femoral arterial return, no-touch anaortic CABG or altered surgical plan.
- Retrograde perfusion from femoral cannulation can dislodge distal atheroma or be unsafe in aortic dissection; axillary perfusion offers different advantages and complications.
- The principle is to minimise **manipulation of diseased aorta**, not routinely to use one cannulation site for everyone.

## Hypothermia: why cool, and what are the costs?

- Temperature determines enzyme kinetics and the rate at which tissues consume O₂.
- A traditional approximation is a **6–7% fall in cerebral oxygen metabolism per 1°C** fall, but this is not linear across the entire temperature range.
- Controlled hypothermia extends tolerance of temporary reduced cerebral/visceral perfusion, making complex aortic operations possible.
- It is not a substitute for adequate oxygen delivery on ordinary CPB, nor does it prevent embolism.

- **The 2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline defines cooling categories (core temperature):**

| Classification | Temperature | Typical context |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | 28.1–34°C | Many routine operations or selected cerebral-protection strategies |
| High-moderate | 24.1–28°C | Selected aortic surgery, often with cerebral perfusion |
| Low-moderate | 20.1–24°C | Complex arch surgery depending on cerebral perfusion plan |
| Deep | 14.1–20°C | Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA) for selected arch/aortic procedures |

**Trade-offs:**

- Hypothermia reduces oxygen consumption but causes platelet dysfunction, delayed coagulation, altered drug metabolism, electrolyte shifts and cardiac irritability.
- Rewarming can cause cerebral hyperthermia, increase oxygen demand and contribute to gaseous microemboli.
- Maintain controlled arterial–venous/heat-exchanger gradients according to perfusion protocol; the updated CPB guideline advises that the heat exchanger–arterial inflow difference should not exceed **10°C** during cooling/rewarming.
- Use appropriate nasopharyngeal and bladder/rectal/core sites because rapid brain and slower body temperature changes diverge.

## Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA): rationale and steps

**The purpose is cerebral and end-organ protection during a period when normal systemic circulation must stop**, typically for open distal ascending aorta or arch work in which a cross-clamp/cannula would obstruct the field. This is not ‘the same as cardioplegia’ and not ‘ECMO’.

- **1.** Establish CPB, anticoagulation and cerebral monitoring; cool slowly to the agreed deep-hypothermic range (often **18–20°C**, patient/protocol dependent).
- **2.** At adequate cooling and myocardial protection, stop systemic pump flow for the necessary period, while the surgeon opens/repairs the arch; provide agreed selective **antegrade cerebral perfusion** (ACP) or retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP) if used.
- **3.** Re-establish perfusion as soon as feasible, de-air meticulously, rewarm slowly and avoid overshoot hyperthermia or large arterial–venous temperature gradients.
- **4.** Monitor return of cerebral oximetry/electrical activity, coagulation and renal/neurological complications.

**Safe time is not a single magic number:**

- Isolated DHCA without perfusion has limited cerebral protection, with guideline discussion suggesting neurological risk rises substantially beyond approximately **30–40 minutes**.
