items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
These are not merely names to memorise. For each, know **who was studied, what intervention was compared, what the primary outcome showed, and what you must not over-extrapolate**. Trials from a non-cardiac surgery population or from acute MI shock do not automatically determine postcardiotomy practice.

| Trial | Topic | Key message |
|---|---|---|
| [CORONARY](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1601564) (Lamy et al., NEJM 2016, five-year follow-up) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 4,752 patients randomised to off- versus on-pump CABG. The five-year composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% versus 23.6%** (no significant difference). Use: operator experience, completeness of grafting and patient anatomy are important; off-pump is not uniformly safer. |
| [ROOBY five-year follow-up](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1614341) (Shroyer et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | In a largely male veteran population, five-year death was **15.2% off pump versus 11.9% on pump**. Use: apparently less invasive strategies can produce inferior long-term outcomes in certain contexts; do not generalise one trial to every centre. |
| [GOPCABE](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211666) (Diegeler et al., NEJM 2013) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Elderly patients (≥75 years) having CABG: no major difference in primary composite outcomes at 30 days, although repeat revascularisation differed. Use: the operative method is not chosen on age alone. |
| [ATACAS tranexamic acid](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27774838/) (Myles et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | TXA in coronary surgery reduced blood product use (4,331 vs 7,994 units total) and reoperation for major haemorrhage/tamponade (1.4% vs 2.8%) **but increased seizures** (0.7% vs 0.1%). No statistically significant improvement in its primary composite thrombotic/death outcome. Use: give TXA for blood conservation with a sensible, renal-adjusted dose; seizures are dose/context related. |
| [TRICS III](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818) (Mazer et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 4,860 moderate/high-risk cardiac surgical patients; restrictive RBC transfusion trigger **Hb 7.5 g/dL** was non-inferior to liberal transfusion for death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). Use: restrictive transfusion is reasonable in stable patients; reassess active haemorrhage and ischaemia individually. |
| [TRICS III six-month follow-up](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30146969/) (Mazer et al., NEJM 2018) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Noninferiority of restrictive strategy persisted for the composite clinical outcome at six months. Use: reinforces that using less blood did not worsen the trial’s specified outcomes. |
| [TITRe2](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1403612) (Murphy et al., NEJM 2015) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Postoperative cardiac surgical patients allocated to different restrictive/liberal transfusion thresholds: no significant difference in the primary serious infection/ischaemic composite, but a mortality signal favoured the liberal group, creating earlier uncertainty. Use: contextualise subsequent TRICS III rather than pretending all cardiac transfusion evidence is identical. |
| [BART](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0802395) (Fergusson et al., NEJM 2008) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Compared antifibrinolytic agents in high-risk cardiac surgery; aprotinin associated with concerning mortality compared with lysine analogues. Use: the choice of antifibrinolytic is a safety decision; policy/regulatory status varies by jurisdiction. |
| [SIRS trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26460660/) (Whitlock et al., Lancet 2015) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 7,507 patients on CPB randomised to methylprednisolone versus placebo: no reduction in 30-day mortality or major morbidity. Use: routine prophylactic high-dose corticosteroid is not an evidence-based default for CPB-related inflammatory response. |
| [DECS](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14144) (Dieleman et al., JAMA 2012) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | High-dose dexamethasone in cardiac surgery did not significantly improve its composite major-adverse-event primary outcome, despite some secondary differences. Use: avoid translating anti-inflammatory biomarker changes into assured clinical benefit. |
| [TRACS](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1446) (Hajjar et al., JAMA 2010) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Compared restrictive versus liberal transfusion based on haematocrit after cardiac surgery, finding no significant composite outcome difference in its sample. Use: original transfusion evidence is limited by selected patients, thresholds and statistical power. |
| [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24011548/) (Thiele et al., NEJM 2012; follow-up) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Around 600 patients with MI-related cardiogenic shock and planned early revascularisation: routine IABP did **not** lower 30-day or one-year mortality. Use: indications for IABP now focus on selected bridging physiology rather than a universal survival benefit. |
| [DanGer Shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572) (Møller et al., NEJM 2024) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Selected STEMI-related shock patients: Impella CP decreased 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%**, but increased severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis and renal replacement. Use: selected phenotype and procedure expertise are central; do not apply indiscriminately to postcardiotomy patients. |
| [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227) (Thiele et al., NEJM 2023) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Early VA-ECMO for infarct-related shock did not improve 30-day mortality (**47.8% vs 49.0%**); more bleeding and vascular complications. Use: ‘more flow’ does not guarantee improved survival and imposes a complication burden. |
| [ECMO-CS](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.122.062949) (Ošťádal et al., Circulation 2023) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Immediate VA-ECMO versus early conservative management with rescue ECMO in rapidly deteriorating severe cardiogenic shock; no clear improvement in the primary composite clinical outcome from immediate routine ECMO. Use: timely selected rescue rather than automatic cannulation. |
| [SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199908263410901) (Hochman et al., NEJM 1999) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Early coronary revascularisation in MI-associated cardiogenic shock improved longer-term outcomes even though the 30-day primary mortality difference was not statistically significant. Use: definitive correction of ischaemia remains fundamental; support devices are bridges. |
| [CESAR](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19762075/) (Peek et al., Lancet 2009) | VV-ECMO for respiratory failure | Randomised **referral to an ECMO-capable centre**, not ECMO itself in every patient: 63% versus 47% survived without severe disability at six months. Use: supports specialist service organisation/referral but does not isolate the benefit of the pump alone. |
| [EOLIA](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800385) (Combes et al., NEJM 2018) | VV-ECMO for respiratory failure | Severe ARDS: 60-day mortality **35% ECMO versus 46% control**, P=0.09 for prespecified primary comparison; 28% crossed over from control to rescue ECMO. Use: important signal underpowered/interpreted with crossover, not a definitive positive primary mortality trial. |
| [ERAS Cardiac Society consensus](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2019.1153) (Engelman et al., JAMA Surgery 2019) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | Evidence-based expert recommendations for bundled cardiac enhanced recovery, including prehabilitation, opioid-sparing analgesia, glycaemic control and early mobilisation. Use: fast tracking is a pathway, not just extubation speed; this is consensus and mixed-level evidence rather than one mortality RCT. |
| [Temporary epicardial pacing](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003) (BJA Education 2023 clinical review) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | Not a landmark trial, but a high-yield illustrated teaching publication on pacing modes, threshold checks, capture/sensing and postoperative safety. Use: directly supports practical weaning and the 2026.1 examiner-style pacing question. |
| [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | High-impact evidence synthesis rather than a clinical trial: perfusion, temperature, neurological protection, circuit safety, anticoagulation and myocardial protection. Use: this is the best contemporary synthesis for the technical CPB sections. |

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
## BJA Education reading guide: what to read and why

- **1.** [Principles of cardiopulmonary bypass](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/6/5/176/337119) (BJA Education, 2006). **Start here for the circuit.** Older but exceptionally useful for how venous drainage, pump, oxygenator, heat exchange and cannulation actually work; update practice thresholds from the 2024 CPB guideline.
- **2.** [Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part one — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for heparin, ACT, resistance, rebound and protamine.** Read with the anticoagulation chapter and repeat the protamine-reaction differential aloud.
- **3.** [Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part two — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.008) (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for HIT and alternatives to heparin.** Particularly useful for distinguishing expected post-CPB thrombocytopenia from HIT and managing bivalirudin on bypass.
- **4.** [Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003) (BJA Education, 2023). **Essential for pacing, weaning and ICU capture troubleshooting**; directly relevant to recent ANZCA questions.
- **5.** [Anaesthesia for adult cardiac surgery requiring repeat sternotomy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.10.001) (BJA Education, 2024). **Best set-specific reading for SS_CS 1.15**: CT, previous grafts, emergency access, pre-sternotomy CPB and haemorrhage.
- **6.** [Perioperative care in cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.05.008) (BJA Education, 2021). **Best for fast-track/ERAS concepts**, sedation, analgesia, mobilisation and recovery care.
- **7.** [Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe acute respiratory failure](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001) (BJA Education, 2024). **Practical VV-ECMO overview**: referral, indications, oxygenation/sweep, ventilation and weaning.
- **8.** [Physiology of VV-ECMO, Part 1: terminology, circuits and gas exchange](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.003) (BJA Education, 2026). **Best newer physiology-focused follow-up**; useful for explaining recirculation, blood-flow versus sweep effects and oxygen delivery.
- **9.** [Management of cardiogenic shock after acute coronary syndromes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.01.006) (BJA Education, 2023). **Use for MCS physiology** and the distinction between revascularisation, pressors/inotropy and device-supported circulatory rescue; update device trial interpretation using DanGer Shock/ECLS-SHOCK.
- **10.** [Anaesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.06.004) (BJA Education, 2018). **Useful for procedure variations, cannulation, positioning and TOE**; supplement with contemporary techniques and local practice.
- **11.** [Pulmonary artery catheterisation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.08.003) (BJA Education, 2024). **Useful for haemodynamic phenotyping** of LV versus RV failure and the limits of filling pressures; read selectively alongside the difficult-weaning chapter.
## ANZCA Blue Book, guidelines, examiner reports and reference texts

### ANZCA and Australasian sources

- [ANZCA — Anaesthesia training program curriculum, Appendix Five](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/all-handbooks-and-curriculums/anzca-anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum.pdf). Source of exact Final Examination learning outcomes; the workbook determines which components belong to Set 13.
- [ANZCA — PG27(A), Guideline for major extracorporeal perfusion](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents). Australasian professional framework for safe major extracorporeal perfusion. Local team protocols should operationalise the details.
- [ANZCA — PG46, perioperative echocardiography (2025)](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/anaestrain/ssu/cardiac). Practice and competency standards for echocardiography use; relevant to diagnosis during difficult separation and ICU instability.
- [Hegde S, Pearse B, Santifort K et al. Goal-directed bleeding management: understanding and implementing viscoelastic haemostatic assays across patient blood management](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387). Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025, pages 59 onwards. Core source for applying ROTEM/TEG to actively bleeding patients and avoiding indiscriminate product administration.
- [Johnstone L. The perioperative management of lung transplantation](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/bitstream/11055/1305/5/00_2025_Blue_Book.pdf). Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025. Relevant application of VA-ECMO/CPB versus off-pump support in non-cardiac/thoracic surgery; use as a clinical example, not as a universal transplant protocol.
- [CALS-ANZ: Australasian ANZSCTS/ANZICS cardiothoracic advanced life support](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10692601/). Source for cardiac surgical postoperative arrest management, pacing/shocks and the importance of trained early resternotomy.
- **ANZCA Final Examination chair reports:** 2019.2 Question 1 on DHCA (rationale and physiology); 2016.2 and 2012.2 questions on separation from CPB; 2026.1 Question 7 on epicardial pacing and loss of capture. The reports complement current guidelines but are **exam-expectation sources**, not practice guidelines.
### Current specialty guidelines

- [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on cardiopulmonary bypass in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354) (published 2025). Primary modern reference for circuit, perfusion flow, temperature, cerebral/myocardial protection and CPB safety.
- [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on patient blood management](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae352) (published 2025). Primary reference for transfusion, antifibrinolytics, haemostasis, protamine, VHA and postoperative bleeding.
- [2024 EACTS Guidelines on perioperative medication in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae355). Relevant to preoperative antithrombotic decisions and postoperative resumption of therapy.
- [ELSO guidelines and resources](https://www.elso.org/ecmo-resources/elso-ecmo-guidelines.aspx), including the 2021 adult VV respiratory failure guidance. Relevant to ECMO referral, patient selection, circuit and weaning; centres should use their latest approved protocols.
- [2025 ERC Guidelines — special circumstances in resuscitation](https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/special-circumstances-guidelines). Relevant to arrest in patients early after cardiac surgery, rapid shocks/pacing and expert resternotomy.
- [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/). For current valve-treatment decisions and prosthesis context; the actual cardiac-surgery anaesthetic sequence is explained in Chapters 2–3.
